lessons.title: The resources an aquaculture farm runs on
lessons.html:
Five resource groups

An aquaculture operation combines water, stock, inputs, equipment and people. Managing operational resources means making sure each is available in the right quantity and quality when needed, used efficiently, and protected from loss.

Water

Water is both a resource and the production environment. Track volume available (borehole yield, dam level, river flow), quality, and the volume used per kilogram of fish. In dry years water can limit production, so plan stocking against realistic supply. Water use must stay within the farm's authorisation under the National Water Act 36 of 1998.

Stock

Fish are the farm's main working asset. Manage them through accurate stock records, correct density per unit and planned movement between units.

Consumable inputs

  • Feed: the largest cost; manage stock levels, storage and freshness.
  • Oxygen, lime, salt, disinfectants, remedies and test kit reagents.
  • Fuel for generators and vehicles.
  • Ice and packaging for harvest.

Equipment and infrastructure

Ponds, tanks, raceways, pipework, screens, nets, aerators, pumps, filters, generators, vehicles and scales. Manage them through an asset register, planned maintenance and replacement planning.

People

Staff time and skills are a resource to plan just as carefully: rosters, skills coverage, overtime and training.

Setting stock levels for inputs

  • Usage rate: how much is used per week.
  • Lead time: how long the supplier takes to deliver.
  • Safety stock: extra to cover delays or a usage spike.
  • Reorder point = usage during lead time + safety stock.

Example: if the farm uses 2 tonnes of grower feed a week, delivery takes 2 weeks and you keep 1 week's safety stock, reorder when stock falls to 6 tonnes. Do not overstock perishable items: feed loses vitamin quality and can go mouldy when stored too long.

lessons.title: Using resources efficiently and controlling losses
lessons.html:
Efficiency measures

Measure how much of each resource is used per unit of output, and track it over time.

ResourceMeasure
FeedFeed conversion ratio (feed given / weight gained)
WaterCubic metres per kg of fish produced
EnergykWh or litres of fuel per kg produced
LabourHours per tonne produced
StockSurvival percentage per batch

Common sources of waste

  • Overfeeding, especially in cold weather when appetite drops.
  • Feed spoiled by damp, heat, rodents or birds in poor stores.
  • Aerators running when not needed, or failing when needed.
  • Leaks in pipework and valves.
  • Fish lost to predators, escapes through damaged screens, or theft.
  • Equipment damaged by poor handling or lack of maintenance.

Controls

  • Feed issued against a daily feeding sheet per unit, reconciled with store records weekly.
  • Physical stock counts of feed and chemicals compared with stock cards.
  • Locked stores with controlled keys; chemicals kept separate from feed.
  • Predator nets, secure fencing and security patrols where theft is a risk.
  • Equipment issued and returned by signature.

Allocating scarce resources

When resources are short (feed delayed, water low, a pump down) decide priorities in advance: protect broodstock and high-value batches first, reduce stocking in new units, and communicate clearly to staff what has changed.

Reporting

Produce a short monthly resource report: stock on hand, usage against plan, efficiency measures, losses and actions taken. It supports the budget review and helps the manager decide on investment, for example a more efficient aerator or better feed storage.

Key points

  • Manage water, stock, inputs, equipment and people as linked resources.
  • Reorder point = usage during lead time + safety stock.
  • Track efficiency per kilogram of fish produced.
  • Reconcile feed issued with feeding sheets and stock counts.
  • Set priorities in advance for times when resources are short.
